did_you_know.text: Chapter 18 opens with Bildad the Shuhite speaking, continuing the debate with Job.
Bildad urges his companions to stop talking at length, to reflect and understand—and only then to speak.
Bildad argues that Job cannot expect the earth to change its ways or the rock to be moved from its place for his sake.
One of the chapter’s central images is the extinguishing of the wicked person’s light: his light grows dark, and his lamp no longer shines.
The wicked person’s path is described as dangerous; he is caught in a net and a snare—in other words, in traps along the way.
Terrors surround the wicked person on every side and drive him away, making fear an inseparable part of his fate.
The chapter uses a vivid image of sickness and destruction: the wicked person loses his strength, and even his skin is consumed by death.
The wicked person’s tent is portrayed as abandoned and afflicted, until sulfur is scattered over his dwelling—a picture of complete destruction.
The image of a tree emphasizes the wicked person’s downfall: his roots dry up below, and his branches are cut off above.
At the end, the wicked person’s memory is described as being erased from the earth; he has no descendants or survivors, and he causes shock among future generations.
